text: Benny and Rick both get a one-thousand-dollar bonus.
Benny buys a new phone. On a credit card.
Rick puts his in an index fund.
Thirty years later, the gap between them is wild.
Benny's phone is awesome. But it starts losing value the day he opens the box.
Then the credit card bill shows up.
Twenty-two percent interest. He pays fifty bucks a month.
Twenty-five months later, he's paid about twelve hundred sixty dollars for a one-thousand-dollar phone.
Rick's thousand? It just sits there. Boring.
But over the long run, the stock market has averaged about ten percent a year.
At that pace, one thousand turns into about seventeen thousand in thirty years.
Card interest compounds against you. Index funds compound for you.
Here's the catch. Some years it drops over thirty percent, and Rick has to sit still and not panic.
That's why Rick keeps an emergency fund, so a surprise bill never forces him to sell low.
And Benny? He's not dumb. He needed a phone.
The smart move: buy it with cash, and invest the next bonus.
Do that with every bonus, and the gap keeps growing.
Same thousand dollars. One paid the bank. One paid the future.
Which one are you? Comment below.
